title: Washington's weirdest unexplained phenomena
excerpt: It’s spooky season again, and that means scary stories. Sometimes the scariest stories aren’t the ones involving goblins and ghouls, but the real-life mysteries that seemingly no one can explain.
content:
It’s spooky season again, and that means scary stories. Sometimes the scariest stories aren’t the ones involving goblins and ghouls, but the real-life mysteries that seemingly no one can explain.

Washington state has its fair share of unexplained phenomena, ranging from mythical monsters to geographical oddities. Each instance serves as a reminder that we don’t know as much as we think we do. Here are seven unexplained phenomena from the Evergreen State:

What were the Oakville blobs in Western Washington?

The mystery of the Oakville blobs continues to inspire speculation even decades after the event. In 1994, the small town of Oakville experienced precipitation like never before. Rather than a strong rain or hail as expected, residents discovered a gelatinous, translucent substance falling from the sky. Some people and animals reportedly got sick after touching the blobs. The state investigated the substance, but nothing conclusive came of the testing.

More than 30 years later, there is still no definitive answer as to what the blobs were. Some believe military testing was the root cause, others look beyond to “star jelly,” or a substance believed to come from meteor showers and other astronomical sources. With all testing samples long gone, it’s likely we’ll never know what fell on Oakville in 1994.

Netflix’s “Files of the Unexplained” showcased the Oakville blobs in 2024. Other shows and popular social media series have also explored the phenomenon, such as the Watcher YouTube series “Mystery Files.”

Why do feet wash up on Salish Sea beaches?

“Files of the Unexplained” also mentioned another Washington state mystery: the number of disembodied feet, still in sneakers, that have washed up on beaches around the Salish Sea. In the last 20 or so years, around two dozen feet have been found on the shore.

Some believe the occurrences have increased in recent years, though experts speculate that the number of discoveries has simply grown along with social media coverage. The owners of some of the feet have been identified using DNA analysis. The majority belong to missing people who reportedly died by suicide or in accidents. Others are too decomposed to link to a particular person.

The sheer volume of people living and recreating around the Puget Sound contributes to a large number of corpses ending up in the waters for various reasons, experts told Vox in 2017. These bodies eventually become food for ocean scavengers, which generally start with the softest parts of the body, often above the ankle. This can lead to extremities getting detached.

Sneakers, the most buoyant shoe option, then carry detached feet to shore due to the flow of water. Some believe there are more sinister reasons behind the unaccompanied appendages, it’s the specific conditions surrounding the Salish Sea that mostly likely lead to the discovery of more feet on local beaches.

What are the Mima Mounds in Thurston County?

Mima Mounds Natural Area Preserve showcases another natural phenomenon that has stumped scientists for decades. A series of dirt mounds measuring up to 7 feet high and 40 feet across, the phenomenon has been described as soil or prairie pimples.

Geological features like the Mima Mounds have been found across the world, but there’s still no conclusive explanation as to how they occur. According to the Washington State Department of Natural Resources, possible explanations include seismic activity and glacial impacts. Visiting the Mima Mounds preserve is the best way to see the hills of silt, sand and pebbles, though other sets appear in the area.

How does Gravity Hill in Prosser work?

On the rural outskirts of Prosser in Eastern Washington, you can find Gravity Hill. If you drive up to the bottom of the hill, then put your car in neutral, you are naturally pulled to the top of the hill and down the road. There are several theories as to why that happens.

The most ominous, and far-fetched, is that ghost children push your car up the hill.

Some people recommend dusting the back of your car with dirt or flour before you start your trek on Gravity Hill, claiming small handprints will be visible after your trip. Others suggest you’re experiencing a magnetic reaction in the landscape. Another, more popular theory — one that’s been investigated by scientists — is that it’s an optical illusion.

While on ground level, you wouldn’t be able to discern if the hill you’re on is actually part of a larger hill. The theory essentially is that being on a hill within a hill would cause this movement, as you’d naturally follow the flow of the larger hill. Some believe that this theory has no credence in Prosser, based on elevation testing.

At this point, no one knows exactly why Gravity Hill moves cars the way it does.

What is Mel’s Hole in Central Washington?

Speculation about the existence of Mel’s Hole has gone on since the late 1990s. That’s when a man who identified himself as Mel Waters called a national radio show about a seemingly bottomless hole on his Kittitas County property. Mel and others claimed that the hole had fantastical powers, including the ability to resurrect dead animals.

Theories started popping up, ranging from alien involvement to military disposal. However, no one has ever been able to credibly confirm the hole exists. A vague location has been referenced, but it includes a fairly large area of private property on Manastash Ridge.

The Yakima Herald-Republic investigated the claims by looking into county records and failed to find anyone named Mel Waters living in the area.

Geologists wrote off the possibility of Mel’s Hole after claims that it was at least 80,000 feet deep. Experts say this is physically impossible. Regardless, since the first call from Mel Waters, there have been news articles, documentaries, books and many discussions dedicated to the story.

Has Bigfoot been spotted in Washington state?

Bigfoot, the famous cryptid who resembles a giant hairy ape, has reportedly been spotted across Pacific Northwest forests, including those in Washington state. According to the Bigfoot Field Researchers Organization’s database, Washington state has had more Bigfoot sightings than any other state, with more than 700 total reports.

The Washington National Guard even has information on the legend, including the fact that “Sasquatch” is derived from the Salish word “Sasquits.” Multiple counties have enacted legal protections for the legendary creature, imposing fines and other punishments for anyone who kills a sasquatch.

Some areas in Washington state are more popular for Sasquatch sightings than others, including the Olympic Peninsula, surrounding Lake Wenatchee, the Oregon Butte area and around Mount Rainier.

There have been numerous conventions and Sasquatch-dedicated events in Washington state over the years, including Bigfoot Con and the Metaline Falls Bigfoot Festival. Despite many rumors and reported sightings, however, the existence of this species has never been conclusively confirmed.

Why are so many UFOs spotted in Washington state?

Bigfoot isn’t the only paranormal sighting associated with the Evergreen State. There’s also been a high frequency of sightings of unidentified flying objects in Washington state. UFOs are now formally known as unidentified anomalous phenomena — UAP — in an effort to ease the stigma around such sightings.

Whatever you call them, sightings of unexplained aircraft are common in Washington. In fact, Washington state regularly ranks high in studies analyzing which states have the most sightings, both by sheer volume and by capita.

Perhaps the most popular spot is around Mount Rainier, where perhaps the most well-known UAP sighting in Washington state took place. In 1947, private pilot Kenneth Arnold reported seeing nine shiny objects moving at fast speeds near the mountain. Arnold’s description of the strange aircraft led to widespread use of the term “flying saucer.”

Due to the nationwide appeal of the story, and subsequent government investigations, some believe Arnold’s sighting set off decades of public fascination with UAPs. The Evergreen State has been a hotbed for such sightings ever since.
